before.content_html:
The First Raids: Lindisfarne 793

In 793, Vikings attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne off the Northumbrian coast, killing monks, stealing treasure and carrying off slaves. The scholar Alcuin, writing from the Frankish court, called it a catastrophe without precedent in English history. Lindisfarne was not just a place of worship — it was one of the most important centres of Christian learning in northern Europe. The attack sent shockwaves across the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.

The raids that followed were driven by multiple factors. Population pressure in Scandinavia pushed younger sons to seek land and wealth abroad. Advances in longship technology allowed Vikings to navigate shallow rivers as well as open seas, striking far inland. Anglo-Saxon England, divided into rival kingdoms and rich in monasteries and trading towns, was an attractive and vulnerable target.

Key Fact

The raid on Lindisfarne in 793 is traditionally seen as the start of the Viking Age in England. It was a major monastic centre, making it rich in portable silver and gold and symbolically devastating when attacked.

The Great Heathen Army and Alfred’s Response

Raiding gave way to conquest in 865–78 when the Great Heathen Army arrived under leaders including Halfdan and Ivar the Boneless. By 875 they had taken York (Jorvik), destroyed the kingdoms of Northumbria and East Anglia, and killed King Edmund of East Anglia. Only Wessex stood unconquered.

Alfred, King of Wessex, was driven to the Somerset marshes by 878 before regrouping and defeating the Viking leader Guthrum at the Battle of Edington. The subsequent Treaty of Wedmore established the Danelaw, dividing England between Alfred’s Wessex and Danish-controlled territory. Alfred then fortified his kingdom with a network of burhs (defended towns) and reorganised the fyrd (local militia) to prevent further collapse.

Alfred’s response to the Viking threat was systematic. He divided the fyrd so that one half could always be on campaign while the other worked the fields, ending the problem of armies dispersing during harvest. He built or strengthened thirty burhs across Wessex, each no more than twenty miles apart, so that no one was far from a defensible refuge. He also invested in a small fleet — an early form of naval defence. These reforms were recorded in the “Burghal Hidage,” a document listing each burh and the number of men required to defend it.

Alfred’s son Edward the Elder and granddaughter Æthelflaed, Lady of the Mercians, continued this campaign of reconquest. By 954 the last Viking king of York had been expelled and England was effectively unified under the West Saxon dynasty for the first time.

Danegeld and the Reign of Æthelred

A new wave of Viking attacks in the 980s–1010s tested Anglo-Saxon defences severely. King Æthelred (known later as “the Unready” — a corruption of the Old English “un-ræd,” meaning poorly counselled) chose to pay Danegeld rather than fight, handing over vast sums of silver. The Battle of Maldon in 991, where the ealdorman Byrhtnoth was killed, became a byword for heroic but futile resistance.

Æthelred’s policy was controversial. Danegeld drained the treasury and arguably encouraged further raiding by demonstrating England’s willingness to pay. His order in 1002 to massacre Danish settlers on St Brice’s Day provoked the Danish king Sweyn Forkbeard to launch a full invasion. By 1013 Æthelred had fled to Normandy. Sweyn’s son Cnut became King of England in 1016 and ruled capably until his death in 1035.

Cnut ruled a North Sea empire encompassing England, Denmark and Norway. He governed England using Anglo-Saxon law and institutions, married Æthelred’s widow Emma of Normandy, and was regarded as a strong, legitimate king. Viking settlement left lasting marks on England: place names ending in “-by” (village), “-thorpe” (farm) and “-thwaite” (meadow) are evidence of Scandinavian settlement across the north and east. Words such as “sky,” “window,” “knife” and “law” entered English from Old Norse.

Historians distinguish between Viking raiders, traders and settlers. Many Scandinavians who came to England did so to farm, trade or seek service with Anglo-Saxon lords rather than to plunder. The archaeological evidence from York (Jorvik) shows a thriving commercial town with craft workshops, not simply a military garrison.

Key Fact

After Edington (878), Alfred reorganised the fyrd on a rota system and built a network of burhs (fortified towns) across Wessex. These two reforms — military and defensive — are the key reasons Wessex survived further Viking attacks.

Stamford Bridge and the End of the Viking Age

In September 1066, King Harold Godwinson of England faced a Norwegian invasion led by Harald Hardrada and his own brother Tostig. Harold marched his army north at extraordinary speed and defeated the Norwegians at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066 — a crushing victory. Harald Hardrada was killed. Of the 300 ships that had carried the Norwegian army to England, reportedly only 25 returned.

Stamford Bridge is often seen as the end of the Viking Age in England. But Harold had no time to celebrate: news arrived almost immediately that William of Normandy had landed in the south. Harold’s exhausted army marched south, and three weeks later he was dead at Hastings. The Viking threat had ended — but it had cost England its last Anglo-Saxon king.

before.content_html:
The Battle of Hastings and Norman Conquest

On 14 October 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings. Harold was killed — traditionally said to have been struck by an arrow — and the English army collapsed. William marched to London and was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. The Norman Conquest was one of the most transformative events in English history, replacing the Anglo-Saxon ruling class with Norman lords almost entirely within a generation.

English resistance did not collapse immediately. The north of England rose repeatedly in 1067–70. In 1069, a Danish fleet landed in support of the northern rebels, and William responded with the devastating Harrying of the North. Contemporary accounts describe mass death from starvation and cold across Yorkshire. Chronicler Orderic Vitalis, writing in the early twelfth century, described the land lying uncultivated for nine years and thousands of bodies left to rot. Historians continue to debate the scale of the destruction, but Domesday Book (1086) records large areas of Yorkshire as “waste,” confirming long-term depopulation.

Key Fact

William I’s Harrying of the North (1069–70) was a deliberate scorched-earth campaign to crush northern resistance. Domesday Book (1086) records extensive areas of Yorkshire as “waste,” suggesting lasting depopulation and economic destruction.

Castle-Building and Military Control

The Normans used castles as instruments of conquest and control. The earliest were motte-and-bailey castles: quick to build using forced local labour and highly effective as garrison points. Within a decade of 1066, hundreds had been built across England. Some, like the Tower of London, were rebuilt in stone as permanent symbols of Norman power.

Castles served multiple functions: they housed garrisons to suppress rebellion, provided bases for rapid military response, and demonstrated the physical dominance of Norman lords over the surrounding population. They also disrupted existing communities — in some towns, houses were demolished to make way for castle construction. The castle-building programme was funded partly through the feudal system.

The Norman feudal system reorganised English society around military obligation. The king held all land and granted it to tenants-in-chief (great barons and bishops) in exchange for knight service — the provision of armed knights for royal campaigns. Barons sublet land to knights, who in turn held peasant farmers (villeins) who worked the land and owed labour services.

The Domesday Book of 1086 recorded all landownership in England, allowing William to assess who held land, how much military service they owed and what taxes could be raised. It was the most detailed administrative survey in medieval Europe and gave the Crown an unprecedented picture of its resources.

Feudal Breakdown: Stephen and The Anarchy

The feudal system depended on a strong king keeping barons loyal through a mixture of reward and force. When Henry I died in 1135 without a male heir, England plunged into civil war between his daughter, Empress Matilda, and his nephew, Stephen. The period 1135–54 is known as The Anarchy because of the breakdown of royal authority.

Contemporary chronicler the “Peterborough Chronicler” described barons building unlicensed castles and oppressing the common people with impunity — “it was said openly that Christ and his saints slept.” The civil war demonstrated a fundamental weakness in the feudal system: when competing claimants each sought baronial support by granting concessions, central authority collapsed and lords acted as local warlords. Order was only restored when Stephen agreed the Treaty of Wallingford (1153), recognising Matilda’s son Henry as his heir.

A second major feudal breakdown came under King John (1199–1216). John lost Normandy to France at the Battle of Bouvines (1214), making him deeply unpopular with barons who had estates on both sides of the Channel. His demands for money — through scutage (a tax in place of military service) and arbitrary fines — broke the feudal compact. In 1215, barons forced John to sign Magna Carta, which placed limits on royal taxation and arbitrary imprisonment.

John repudiated Magna Carta almost immediately. The First Barons’ War (1215–17) followed, with rebel barons inviting the French prince Louis to claim the English throne. John’s death in 1216 changed the situation: his nine-year-old son Henry III reissued Magna Carta as a peace offering, and the regent William Marshal defeated the French at the Battle of Lincoln (1217), ending the war. Magna Carta survived as a foundation document limiting royal power.

Key Fact

The feudal system was built on the relationship between king and barons. When that relationship broke down — through disputed succession (The Anarchy) or royal overreach (John) — the same barons who were supposed to provide military service instead turned their forces against the Crown.

before.content_html:
Edward I and the Welsh and Scottish Wars

Between 1277 and 1283, Edward I conquered Wales in two campaigns, building a network of concentric stone castles — Caernarfon, Harlech, Conwy, Beaumaris — that have been described as the most ambitious military architecture in medieval Europe. The castles were planted in Welsh territory as garrison points and symbols of English domination. Welsh resistance continued, including a major revolt in 1294–95, but Edward’s strategic use of castle-building and supplied garrisons proved decisive.

Scotland proved harder to subdue. Edward I intervened in a succession dispute in 1296, deposed the Scottish king John Balliol and declared himself overlord. Scottish resistance under William Wallace (defeated at Falkirk 1298) and later Robert Bruce (crowned 1306) prolonged the conflict. The First War of Scottish Independence continued until the Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton (1328), which recognised Scottish independence under Robert I. Edward I’s Scottish campaigns were financially ruinous and politically divisive, demonstrating the limits of English military power even against a smaller neighbour.

Key Fact

Edward I conquered Wales using a combination of castle-building (Caernarfon, Harlech) and military campaigns in 1277 and 1282–83. His Scottish campaigns (1296–1307) ultimately failed: Scotland remained independent under Robert Bruce, confirmed by the Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton in 1328.

The Hundred Years’ War and Changing Warfare

The Hundred Years’ War (1337–1453) between England and France was driven by English kings’ claims to the French throne and disputes over territory. It transformed how wars were fought. The traditional feudal levy — knights and foot soldiers serving for forty days per year under feudal obligation — was increasingly replaced by the indenture system, in which captains contracted with the Crown to provide set numbers of soldiers for pay. Professional, paid armies were more reliable and easier to supply on long campaigns abroad.

The English longbow was the defining weapon of the early phases of the war. Battles such as Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) showed English and Welsh archers inflicting devastating casualties on French cavalry. At Crécy, Edward III’s archers fired at rates modern estimates put at ten to twelve arrows per minute, breaking repeated French cavalry charges. The tactical dominance of the longbow undermined the social prestige of mounted knights and accelerated the shift towards infantry-based armies.

At Agincourt on 25 October 1415, Henry V’s army of perhaps 6,000–9,000 men defeated a French force estimated at three to five times its size. The English positioned themselves between two woods, forcing the French to advance along a narrow muddy field that negated their numerical advantage. Longbowmen on the flanks poured arrows into tightly packed French ranks. English casualties were reported as very low; French knights died in the thousands.

The Treaty of Troyes (1420) recognised Henry V as heir to the French throne. He died in 1422, aged 35, before inheriting France. The war continued under his son Henry VI, who eventually lost almost all English territory in France. Joan of Arc’s relief of Orleans in 1429 turned the tide decisively in France’s favour. By 1453 England retained only Calais from its French territories. The Hundred Years’ War ended not with a treaty but with England’s effective military defeat.

The Financial Cost of Medieval War

Sustained warfare was enormously expensive. Edward I’s Welsh and Scottish campaigns required repeated taxation that strained his relationship with Parliament. The Hundred Years’ War cost the English Crown vast sums: soldiers had to be paid, ships requisitioned, supplies shipped to France and castles garrisoned. To raise money, kings increasingly relied on Parliamentary grants of taxation, which gave Parliament growing leverage over royal policy.

Chevauchée tactics — systematic raiding and burning of French countryside — were used by English armies to destroy French tax revenues and force battle, but they also devastated the civilian populations of regions where armies operated. Contemporaries recorded the destruction of hundreds of villages, the slaughter of livestock and the abduction of people for ransom during English campaigns in France.

For ordinary people in regions where armies campaigned, war meant disruption, destruction and death far beyond the battlefield. In Wales, the construction of Edward I’s castles required forced labour and the displacement of Welsh communities. In France, years of English chevauchée campaigns left landscapes stripped of crops and livestock. The Hundred Years’ War coincided with the Black Death (1348–50), compounding the human cost across northern France and southern England.

In England itself, the war’s impact was felt through heavy taxation to fund campaigns, disruption to the wool trade when France was an enemy, and the losses of families who sent men abroad on campaign. The war also transformed social attitudes: the longbow victories at Crécy and Agincourt became sources of national pride, and chronicles celebrated English military prowess, laying the groundwork for later nationalist mythology around these battles.

Key Fact

The indenture system replaced the feudal levy during the Hundred Years’ War. Captains contracted with the Crown to provide paid soldiers. This was better for long overseas campaigns because paid men could serve indefinitely, unlike feudal levies who were only obligated for forty days per year.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Edward I used castle-building to control Wales (1277–83) but his Scottish campaigns (1296–1328) ultimately failed, demonstrating the limits of English military power.
  • The Hundred Years’ War (1337–1453) shifted English armies from feudal levies to the indenture system of paid professional soldiers, and the longbow proved decisive at Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415).
  • War was ruinously expensive, gave Parliament growing power over taxation and devastated civilian populations in Wales, Scotland and France.

before.content_html:
Elizabeth I and the Threat from Spain

By the 1560s, England and Spain were on a collision course. Religious conflict — Philip II of Spain was a committed Catholic, Elizabeth I a Protestant — combined with commercial rivalry over Atlantic trade routes. The trigger for open conflict came in 1568, when Spanish forces seized English merchant ships at San Juan de Ulúa in the Gulf of Mexico, stranding John Hawkins and a young Francis Drake. Drake vowed personal revenge, and Elizabeth increasingly backed privateers to harass Spanish shipping without formally declaring war.

Privateers blurred the line between piracy and state warfare. Elizabeth issued “letters of marque” authorising attacks on Spanish vessels. The Crown took a share of captured treasure while maintaining plausible deniability in diplomacy. Francis Drake’s circumnavigation of the globe (1577–80) was partly a raiding voyage: he plundered Spanish ports on the Pacific coast of South America, returning with treasure worth perhaps £600,000 — more than the Crown’s entire annual revenue. Elizabeth knighted him on the deck of his ship at Deptford.

Key Fact

Privateers were Crown-licensed sea captains permitted to attack enemy ships for profit. Elizabeth used them to harass Spanish trade and plunder treasure without formally going to war — preserving diplomatic flexibility while gaining wealth and weakening Spain.

The Spanish Armada 1588

Philip II launched the Spanish Armada in the summer of 1588: 130 ships intended to escort the Duke of Parma’s army from the Netherlands to invade England. The plan required precise coordination. English ships under Lord Howard of Effingham and Drake harried the Armada up the Channel in a series of engagements. At Gravelines, English fireships sent into the anchored fleet caused panic and dispersal. The Armada attempted to return to Spain by sailing around Scotland and Ireland; storms wrecked perhaps two-thirds of the fleet. Around 50 ships and perhaps 15,000 Spanish sailors and soldiers died.

The Armada’s failure became a defining moment of Elizabethan propaganda. Elizabeth’s speech at Tilbury — whether delivered as recorded or not — presented her as a warrior queen personally leading her people. Commemorative medals were struck with the motto “God blew, and they were scattered.” The reality was that England had been in genuine danger: the Armada was not defeated so much as frustrated by English tactics, Spanish planning failures and storms. The Anglo-Spanish War continued until 1604.

Privateering had mixed effects on English society. For merchants and investors in port towns like Plymouth and Bristol, it offered the prospect of enormous profits. Drake’s circumnavigation was backed by a syndicate of investors including Elizabeth herself. Captured Spanish silver flowed into English commerce, stimulating trade and investment.

However, privateering also increased insecurity. Spanish reprisals targeted English merchants. Coastal towns lived under threat of Spanish raids — in 1595, a Spanish force landed in Cornwall and burned Mousehole, Newlyn and Penzance. The cost of defending against Spanish attack meant constant demands for Parliamentary taxation. The career of John Hawkins illustrates the period’s moral complexity: he was both an early English slave trader and a key reformer of the Royal Navy who helped build the fleet that faced the Armada.

Elizabeth’s Wars and Parliament

Tudor maritime warfare strained the relationship between Crown and Parliament. War was expensive — the Armada crisis alone required emergency taxation — and Parliament controlled the purse strings. Elizabeth famously avoided calling Parliament when she could, but military necessity forced her hand repeatedly. The wars with Spain between 1585 and 1604 cost the Crown millions of pounds and led to significant crown debt.

Elizabeth managed Parliament through a combination of personal charisma, selective concession and the projection of royal prestige. The Armada victory strengthened her position, allowing her to resist Parliamentary pressure on religious and succession questions. But the later years of her reign saw growing tension with Parliament over royal prerogatives and the cost of the Irish wars (1594–1603), where England fought a prolonged and expensive campaign against Hugh O’Neill, Earl of Tyrone. Monopolies — royal grants giving favoured courtiers exclusive rights over certain trades — became a flashpoint, with Parliament in 1601 forcing Elizabeth to concede their revocation.

In 1596, an English fleet under Essex and Howard raided the Spanish port of Cádiz, destroying the harbour and Spanish treasure ships. It was a daring propaganda success, though the anticipated treasure largely eluded capture. English attempts to establish a permanent New World colony in this period — Roanoke (1585–90) — failed, though they demonstrated English ambitions that would be realised under James I at Jamestown (1607).

The New World context reveals the intersection of war and commerce in Elizabethan foreign policy. Attacking Spanish silver fleets disrupted the money supply that funded Philip II’s armies in the Netherlands and his plans against England. Elizabeth’s support for Dutch Protestants fighting Spain (from 1585) transformed England from a reactive defender into an active participant in a continental Protestant cause — raising the ideological stakes of the conflict beyond mere commercial rivalry.

Key Fact

The wars with Spain required repeated Parliamentary taxation and strained Crown finances. Elizabeth managed Parliament through personal authority and the prestige of the Armada victory, but was forced to concede the revocation of monopolies in 1601. The wars demonstrated how military necessity gave Parliament leverage over the Crown.

before.content_html:
The Border Landscape and Its People

The Anglo-Scottish border in the sixteenth century was not a fixed, clearly patrolled line but a lawless zone of upland moorland, shifting loyalties and endemic raiding. Border Reivers were the principal actors: families — Armstrongs, Elliots, Grahams, Nixons, Scotts — who raided across the border for cattle, sheep and ransomable prisoners with little distinction between English and Scottish victims. Reiver raids could strike at any time; a whole community’s livestock might vanish overnight. The practice was so embedded that it generated its own legal term: “blackmail” (originally protection money paid to reivers) and the phrase “bereaved” (to have been raided and robbed).

The borderlands were administered in three zones on each side: the West March, Middle March and East March. Each was governed by a Warden of the Marches, a powerful noble appointed by the Crown. Wardens held March Days — formal meetings at the border where disputes were settled and stolen goods returned. The system was supposed to provide order, but wardens were often themselves reiver clan members or in alliance with reiver families, making impartial enforcement difficult.

Key Fact

Border Reivers were raiding families from both sides of the Anglo-Scottish border. Wardens of the Marches were royal officials meant to enforce order, but their effectiveness was limited by their own connections to reiver families.

Warfare on the Borders: Flodden to Pinkie

Alongside the persistent low-level violence of reiving, the border region was also the site of pitched battles between English and Scottish armies. At Flodden in 1513, an English army under the Earl of Surrey defeated and killed James IV of Scotland and much of the Scottish nobility. Flodden was a catastrophe for Scotland — the king and thousands of men dead in a single afternoon — but it did not end the border problem. Scottish raiding continued, and English armies mounted periodic punitive invasions known as “rough wooings” in the 1540s, intended to force a marriage alliance between the young Mary Queen of Scots and the future Edward VI.

The Battle of Pinkie (1547) was one of the last major Anglo-Scottish engagements before the Union of Crowns. English forces defeated the Scots at Musselburgh in one of the first modern battles to combine massed infantry fire from handguns with cavalry and artillery. But military victory did not translate into political settlement. The Scots sought and received French support, and Mary was sent to France, frustrating English plans for a union by marriage. The border remained a zone of intermittent conflict throughout the mid-Tudor period.

For ordinary people in the border counties, warfare was a lived reality rather than a distant policy concern. Farms were attacked repeatedly; livestock — the main form of wealth in an upland pastoral economy — was the principal target. Communities built peel towers as refuges against raids. Wealthy families might negotiate arrangements with reiver clans, paying protection money (blackmail) rather than face repeated attack.

The violence was not simply chaotic. Reiving operated according to unwritten codes: taking goods was acceptable, killing without reason was not; ransoms were standard practice. The border community had developed its own semi-legal customs because the formal legal systems of England and Scotland were too distant and too slow to provide justice. This parallel informal legal culture was one reason the borderlands were so resistant to royal control throughout the sixteenth century.

The Union of Crowns and the End of Border Warfare

The Union of Crowns in 1603, when James VI of Scotland became James I of England, changed the border’s status fundamentally. What had been a frontier between two kingdoms became an internal region of a single Crown. James declared the border counties a “Middle Shires” and set about eliminating reiving through a sustained campaign of force. A joint Anglo-Scottish commission was established; reiver families faced hanging, transportation and the breaking up of their clans.

The Armstrong clan, one of the most powerful reiver families, was particularly targeted. Hundreds were executed or transported to Ireland in the early seventeenth century. By 1610, the pacification of the borders was largely complete. The border region, which had sustained a distinctive culture of violence and semi-independence for centuries, was integrated into the wider political and legal order of Britain within a decade of the union. The speed of this change illustrates how the border had been sustained as a lawless zone largely by the existence of two competing state authorities — remove the frontier and the reivers had nowhere left to operate.

The Anglo-Scottish border was never simply a local problem — it was part of the wider strategic competition between England, Scotland and France. Scotland’s alliance with France (the “Auld Alliance”) meant that a hostile Scotland represented a second front against England whenever England was at war with France. Henry VIII’s Italian wars, for example, were accompanied by Scottish raiding that culminated at Flodden (1513). Securing the northern border was therefore an ongoing strategic priority for Tudor governments.

The Rough Wooing policy of the 1540s — trying to force Scotland into a Protestant union with England through military pressure — failed diplomatically but contributed to a gradual shift in Scottish elite opinion towards England in the later sixteenth century. Protestant reformers in Scotland looked to England for support against French Catholic influence. Elizabeth’s tacit support for Scottish Protestants in 1559–60 helped install a Protestant regime in Edinburgh — making the eventual Union of Crowns possible.

Key Fact

The Union of Crowns (1603) ended border reiving by removing the frontier that had sustained it. James VI/I declared the borderlands ‘Middle Shires’ and used a joint Anglo-Scottish commission to execute, imprison and transport reiver families. The Armstrongs and other major clans were broken within a decade.
before.exam_tip_html: For Change and Continuity essays, border warfare is an excellent example of continuity across time — reiving persisted for over a century despite state efforts to control it — followed by rapid change once the political context shifted with the Union of Crowns. Examiners reward students who explain why the change happened when it did, not just that it happened. For Explain Why questions, practise linking specific detail (March Days, peel towers, Armstrongs) to broader patterns (limits of royal authority, the role of geography and divided sovereignty).

before.content_html:
The Jacobite Cause and the Rising of 1715

The Jacobite cause was born from the Glorious Revolution of 1688, when William III replaced the Catholic James II. James II’s supporters (named after “Jacobus,” the Latin for James) believed the Protestant succession was illegal. The Highland clans of Scotland, many Catholic or Episcopalian, formed the core of Jacobite support. In 1715, following the death of Anne and the Hanoverian succession, James Francis Edward Stuart (“the Old Pretender”) launched a rising in Scotland and northern England. Poor coordination and leadership meant the rising failed — the Pretender arrived in Scotland after the campaign’s decisive moment had passed and left within weeks. The rising was crushed at Sheriffmuir.

The Rising of 1745 was far more dangerous. Charles Edward Stuart (“Bonnie Prince Charlie” or the “Young Pretender”) landed in Scotland in July 1745 with a small French party, raised the Highland clans, defeated a government army at Prestonpans and advanced as far south as Derby — just 125 miles from London. Panic spread through London. Only Charles’s decision to retreat north (against his own preference) prevented a direct march on the capital. The Jacobite army turned back at Derby in December 1745.

Key Fact

In December 1745, Charles Edward Stuart’s army reached Derby — just 125 miles from London. The army retreated north because Charles’s council of war voted against continuing, fearing government forces closing from the south and west. The advance to Derby was the high-water mark of the Jacobite cause.

Culloden and Its Aftermath

The Jacobite Rising ended at the Battle of Culloden on 16 April 1746 — the last pitched battle fought on British soil. The Duke of Cumberland’s government forces, armed with artillery and disciplined musket fire, destroyed the Highland charge in under an hour. Charles escaped to France; around 1,500 Jacobites were killed. Cumberland’s forces pursued Highland fugitives with great brutality, and the repression that followed was systematic. The Disarming Act (1746) banned the wearing of Highland dress and the carrying of weapons; the Heritable Jurisdictions Act (1747) abolished the power of Highland chiefs to hold their own courts, breaking the legal basis of clan authority.

The long-term consequence was the Highland Clearances. In the decades following Culloden, many Highland landowners — including former Jacobite chiefs who had been stripped of their hereditary power and needed new income — converted their estates from subsistence farming to sheep pasture. Thousands of tenant families were evicted, often forcibly, and emigrated to North America and the colonies. The Clearances continued into the nineteenth century, emptying many of the glens that had been densely populated. Contemporary accounts record entire communities herded onto ships or walking to the coast with their possessions.

The Seven Years War (1756–63) was the first truly global conflict, fought across Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines. William Pitt the Elder, as Secretary of State, directed British strategy with a focus on naval supremacy and colonial acquisition rather than European land campaigns. The war was funded by Parliament and the Bank of England; British public debt approximately doubled.

The decisive battle in North America came at the Plains of Abraham (Quebec, 1759), where General James Wolfe led a surprise night ascent of cliffs to attack the French-held city. Both Wolfe and the French commander Montcalm were killed. The capture of Quebec, followed by Montreal (1760), effectively ended French power in North America. The Treaty of Paris (1763) confirmed Britain’s gains: Canada, much of India (via the East India Company’s victories), several Caribbean islands and Florida. Pitt’s imperial strategy had transformed Britain into the dominant global power.

The Impact of the Seven Years War on Britain

The Seven Years War had profound effects on Britain. The public debt crisis required new taxation — including taxes on the American colonies that would contribute to the American War of Independence (1775–83) within a generation. The war created a powerful national identity centred on Protestant British values, commercial enterprise and military prowess: William Hogarth’s prints, the popular press and ballads all celebrated British victories. The union of English and Scottish identities was partly forged in this period: Highland regiments, recruited from the same clans that had fought for the Jacobites in 1745, now served the Crown in Canada and India.

The war also revealed the importance of naval power for an island commercial nation. Pitt’s strategy of blockading France, attacking French colonies and subsidising allies to fight on land in Europe became the template for British grand strategy for over a century. The Royal Navy’s dominance — demonstrated at the Battle of Quiberon Bay (1759), where the French invasion fleet was destroyed — underpinned every British military success of the period.

The memory of Culloden and the Clearances became central to modern Scottish identity. Nineteenth-century Romantic writers, particularly Walter Scott and later the “Balmoralism” associated with Queen Victoria, transformed the Jacobite cause from a defeated political movement into a romantic cultural symbol — the tartan and Highland imagery that now represent Scotland internationally emerged largely from this period of retrospective reinvention.

Historians distinguish carefully between the political reality of the Jacobite risings (a dynastic claim backed by Catholic powers and Highland clans) and the romantic mythology that grew around them. The reality of Culloden — a crushing military defeat followed by systematic repression — and the human suffering of the Clearances are facts documented in contemporary records and estate papers. The romantic version — Bonnie Prince Charlie as tragic hero — emerged decades later and reflects the politics of Victorian identity rather than historical accuracy.

Key Fact

The Treaty of Paris (1763) confirmed Britain’s acquisition of Canada and much of India, following the Seven Years War. It made Britain the dominant global colonial power and established the model of naval-focused imperial strategy associated with William Pitt the Elder.

before.content_html:
The Wars with Revolutionary and Napoleonic France

Britain fought Revolutionary and then Napoleonic France almost continuously from 1793 to 1815. The conflicts had profound effects on British society. The wars required mass mobilisation: the Army expanded enormously, the Navy consumed vast resources, and the Militia Acts brought compulsory service to hundreds of thousands of men at home. Government spending and taxation reached levels previously unprecedented in British history. Income tax was introduced in 1799 by William Pitt the Younger specifically to fund the war, at two shillings in the pound (ten per cent). It was abolished after Waterloo but reintroduced permanently in 1842.

At sea, the Battle of Trafalgar (21 October 1805) saw Admiral Horatio Nelson’s fleet destroy the combined Franco-Spanish fleet off the coast of southern Spain. Nelson was killed by a French marksman during the battle. His death became the subject of national mourning on a scale not seen before in Britain: a state funeral at St Paul’s Cathedral, a lying-in-state, and a cult of heroic sacrifice that shaped Victorian ideas of military honour. Trafalgar ended the threat of a French invasion of Britain and confirmed British naval supremacy for the rest of the century.

Key Fact

Trafalgar (21 October 1805) destroyed the combined Franco-Spanish fleet and ended Napoleon’s hopes of invading Britain. Nelson was killed during the battle, becoming a national hero — his state funeral at St Paul’s Cathedral established new standards of public mourning for military commanders.

Waterloo and Its Consequences

Napoleon was defeated finally at the Battle of Waterloo (18 June 1815), where the Duke of Wellington commanded the Anglo-Dutch army that held the French assault until Prussian reinforcements arrived. Wellington, the son of an Anglo-Irish aristocrat, was the dominant military figure of the age. His victory at Waterloo made him a national hero and eventually Prime Minister. The wars with France, ending with Waterloo, had transformed British military organisation, raised taxation permanently and demonstrated both the costs and benefits of sustained industrial-scale warfare.

The social aftermath of the wars was turbulent. Hundreds of thousands of demobilised soldiers and sailors returned to an economy disrupted by the end of wartime demand. Unemployment and poverty rose sharply. The Corn Laws (1815) kept bread prices high, benefiting landowners but hurting the poor. At Peterloo (16 August 1819), cavalry charged a crowd of around 60,000 people gathered in Manchester to demand parliamentary reform, killing fifteen and injuring hundreds. The name was a deliberate, bitter echo of Waterloo — the men who had fought Napoleon were being cut down by soldiers at home.

The Crimean War (1853–56) was fought by Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire against Russia in the Crimean Peninsula. British army organisation was exposed as chaotic and incompetent: supply failures left soldiers starving in winter conditions, and disease killed far more men than combat. The Charge of the Light Brigade (October 1854) — a cavalry attack on the wrong target, resulting from confused orders — became a symbol of aristocratic military mismanagement and futile heroism in equal measure.

Florence Nightingale transformed military nursing during the Crimean War. Working at the Scutari barracks hospital near Constantinople, she reduced mortality rates dramatically through improved sanitation and hygiene, and used statistical methods to demonstrate the relationship between hospital conditions and death rates. Her work catalysed the professionalisation of nursing and the reform of military medicine, and made her the most famous woman in Britain. Mary Seacole also provided medical care in the Crimea, establishing the ‘British Hotel’ near Balaclava to treat wounded men, though her contributions were largely overlooked for over a century.

The Boer Wars and Questions of Empire

The Boer Wars in South Africa — the First (1880–81) and Second (1899–1902) — challenged Britain’s military reputation and raised difficult moral questions. The first war ended in a British defeat at Majuba Hill (1881), forcing Britain to recognise Boer independence. The second war, triggered by Boer resistance to British imperial expansion in southern Africa, became a prolonged guerrilla conflict. Concentration camps in which Boer civilians and Black African workers were interned led to the deaths of approximately 26,000 Boer women and children and a further estimated 20,000 Black Africans from disease and malnutrition. The camps became a major scandal at home, with Liberal politician Emily Hobhouse’s reports causing public outrage.

The Second Boer War exposed weaknesses in British military preparation. The physical condition of army recruits — many rejected as unfit — alarmed policymakers and contributed to social reform. The revelation that a large proportion of working-class recruits were too unhealthy to serve raised questions about the state’s obligation to maintain the health of its population — concerns that fed into the Liberal welfare reforms of 1906–14 and ultimately contributed to the welfare state of the 1940s. War, in this sense, had long-term domestic political consequences extending far beyond the battlefield.

Peterloo (1819) illustrated how the military culture bred by decades of war could be turned against the domestic population. The Manchester and Salford Yeomanry — a volunteer cavalry unit — charged into a peaceful crowd demanding parliamentary reform. The crowd had been celebrating, with banners and bands; there was no violence before the charge. Fifteen people died; hundreds were injured. The government defended the action and prosecuted the organisers of the meeting. Peterloo radicalised a generation of reformers and contributed to the pressure for the 1832 Reform Act.

The name “Peterloo” was coined immediately by the Manchester Observer newspaper. The bitterness of the allusion — the men who had defeated Napoleon at Waterloo using their sabres on unarmed civilians in a Manchester field — captured widespread outrage. Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote his poem “The Masque of Anarchy” in response, addressing the working people of England and calling them to “Rise like lions after slumber.”

Key Fact

The Second Boer War (1899–1902) concentration camps caused the deaths of approximately 26,000 Boer civilians and around 20,000 Black Africans from disease. Combined with the poor physical fitness of army recruits, the war contributed to Liberal welfare reforms (1906–14) addressing working-class health.
before.exam_tip_html: For Change and Continuity essays, the nineteenth century is rich in evidence for both change and continuity. Change: professionalisation of nursing after Crimea, welfare reform after Boer War, income tax funding mass warfare. Continuity: the costs of war still fell on ordinary people (Peterloo, demobilisation poverty), aristocratic command persisted into Crimea despite incompetence. Examiners reward students who push beyond description to analyse the relationship between war and social or political change — show that war forced the government’s hand.

before.content_html:
The Concept of Total War

The First and Second World Wars introduced a new kind of conflict to British society: total war. Unlike earlier wars fought by professional armies, these conflicts required the mobilisation of the entire population. Factories, farms, women’s labour, food production, transport, communications, even the arts were directed towards the war effort. The state’s power over daily life expanded dramatically in both conflicts, and the boundary between the military “front” and the civilian “home front” largely dissolved.

In the First World War (1914–18), Britain initially relied on voluntary recruitment. Kitchener’s famous poster campaign produced enormous volunteer armies in 1914–15, including the “Pals Battalions” in which men from the same towns or workplaces enlisted together. The catastrophic losses at the Somme (1 July 1916 alone: 57,470 British casualties) and elsewhere meant that voluntary recruitment could not keep pace with attrition. The Military Service Act (1916) introduced conscription for single men aged 18–41, later extended to married men.

Key Fact

The Military Service Act (January 1916) introduced compulsory military service for single men aged 18–41, later extended to married men. It replaced the voluntary recruitment system that had operated since August 1914, reflecting the army’s inability to replace losses at battles like the Somme through volunteers alone.

The Home Front in the First World War

The war transformed the home front. Women took on roles previously restricted to men: working in munitions factories, driving ambulances, managing farms and businesses. David Lloyd George, as Minister of Munitions from 1915 and later Prime Minister, recognised that the war could not be won without mobilising women’s labour on an industrial scale. The “munitionettes” — women working in shell factories — suffered health risks from handling TNT and cordite, and the pay gap between men and women’s work became a political issue. The connection between women’s wartime service and the extension of the franchise was made explicit by many suffragists.

The Representation of the People Act (1918) extended the vote to all men over 21 and women over 30 who met a property qualification. The electorate tripled. The war had made the case for a broader democracy: men who had fought and women who had worked in factories could no longer plausibly be denied political representation. The full equal franchise came in 1928.

The Defence of the Realm Act (DORA), passed on 8 August 1914, gave the government sweeping powers over civilian life: the press was censored, pub opening hours were restricted (early closing laws to curb workers drinking before munitions shifts), clocks were moved to British Summer Time to maximise working hours, and lights were subject to blackout restrictions to frustrate Zeppelin navigation. DORA showed how quickly the state could extend its reach into everyday life in wartime.

Food supply became a critical issue by 1917 when German submarine attacks severely reduced imports. Voluntary rationing proved insufficient; in January 1918 sugar rationing was introduced compulsorily, followed by meat, butter, lard and margarine. Queues at food shops became a feature of daily life. The spectre of starvation — which German civilians actually experienced more severely — became a factor in strategic thinking, demonstrated by the British naval blockade of Germany and by German unrestricted submarine warfare against British shipping.

The Second World War and Deepened Total War

The Second World War (1939–45) extended the logic of total war even further. The Emergency Powers Act (1940) gave the government broader powers than DORA: Ernest Bevin, as Minister of Labour, could direct any person to any work. Conscription was introduced from the outset (September 1939); women aged 19–30 were conscripted for war work or the auxiliary services from 1941. Rationing was comprehensive — food, clothing, petrol and even furniture — and lasted until 1954.

The Blitz brought warfare directly to the civilian population. Between September 1940 and May 1941, German bombers targeted British cities: London was bombed on 57 consecutive nights. Around 43,000 British civilians were killed. Coventry, Plymouth, Liverpool, Birmingham and Bristol suffered severe damage. Around 1.4 million children were evacuated from cities. The shared experience of bombing and rationing contributed to a sense of social solidarity that historians have connected to the political conditions for post-war welfare reform: voters who had experienced total war state intervention expected state provision of healthcare, education and housing.

In November 1942, William Beveridge published his report “Social Insurance and Allied Services,” proposing a universal welfare system that would attack the “five giants” of Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness. The report sold 630,000 copies; it was read by soldiers in the field, debated in Parliament and became the blueprint for the post-war welfare state. The 1945 Labour landslide that defeated Churchill — despite his wartime prestige — reflected public determination to cash in the wartime sacrifice for social improvement.

Ernest Bevin, who had organised labour as wartime Minister of Labour, became Foreign Secretary in the post-war Attlee government. Clement Attlee’s government created the National Health Service (1948), a national insurance system, and embarked on a programme of nationalisation. The welfare state was, in part, the domestic legacy of total war — a society that had accepted state direction of every aspect of life for six years was ready to accept state provision of basic welfare.

Key Fact

Total war transformed the relationship between the state and citizens in three key ways: it massively expanded state power over daily life (DORA 1914, Emergency Powers Act 1940); it extended political rights in recognition of mass participation (Representation of the People Act 1918); and it created the conditions for post-war welfare reform (Beveridge Report 1942, NHS 1948).

before.content_html:
Britain and the Cold War

After 1945, Britain faced a new kind of threat: not an invading army but the possibility of nuclear annihilation. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949; Britain tested its own in 1952. The deterrence logic of MAD meant that both superpowers maintained arsenals capable of destroying civilisation. Britain, as a NATO member, was committed to American nuclear strategy and hosted US air bases. This made Britain both a participant in nuclear deterrence and a potential target.

The Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) was founded in 1958 and quickly became a mass movement. Its annual marches from Aldermaston (the nuclear weapons research centre in Berkshire) to London drew tens of thousands. The philosopher Bertrand Russell and the Canon of St Paul’s, John Collins, were among its founders. CND represented a new form of popular response to warfare — civil society organising against a state military policy rather than supporting it. The movement influenced the Labour Party in the early 1980s, when the party adopted a unilateral disarmament policy before abandoning it after electoral defeat.

Key Fact

CND (Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament) was founded in 1958 and organised annual marches from Aldermaston to London. It represented mass popular opposition to nuclear weapons policy — one of the first large British peace movements of the post-war period.

The Troubles in Northern Ireland 1969–1998

Northern Ireland’s conflict, known as the Troubles, was rooted in the partition of Ireland in 1921 and the deep divisions between the unionist and nationalist communities. The modern Troubles began in 1969 as civil rights protests against discrimination faced by the nationalist community escalated into violence. British troops were deployed in August 1969, initially welcomed by some in the nationalist community as protection against loyalist attacks. The relationship between the Army and nationalist areas deteriorated rapidly.

Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, was a pivotal moment. British paratroopers shot dead fourteen civilian marchers during a civil rights demonstration in Derry/Londonderry. A further person died later from injuries. The Widgery Tribunal (1972) largely exonerated the soldiers. Decades later, the Saville Inquiry (published 2010) concluded that the killings were “unjustified and unjustifiable,” that those shot were not posing a threat and that some soldiers had fired on people who were fleeing or helping the wounded. Prime Minister David Cameron apologised on behalf of the British government on the day the Saville Report was published.

The Provisional IRA conducted a sustained bombing and assassination campaign from 1969 to 1994 aimed at ending British rule in Northern Ireland. Attacks included the Birmingham pub bombings (21 November 1974), which killed 21 people, the Brighton hotel bomb (October 1984) that nearly killed Prime Minister Thatcher, and the Canary Wharf bomb (February 1996) that ended a ceasefire. The Guildford pub bombings (October 1974) killed five. Loyalist paramilitary groups also committed killings, predominantly targeting members of the nationalist community.

The Good Friday Agreement (1998), signed by the British and Irish governments and the main Northern Ireland parties, established a power-sharing assembly and a framework for resolving the conflict through democratic means. Key figures included John Hume (SDLP), Gerry Adams (Sinn Féin), David Trimble (Ulster Unionist Party) and Mo Mowlam as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland. The Agreement received 71% support in a referendum in Northern Ireland and 94% in the Republic of Ireland. The Troubles are estimated to have killed approximately 3,500 people over thirty years.

The Iraq War 2003

On 15 February 2003, approximately one million people marched through London to oppose the planned invasion of Iraq — one of the largest demonstrations in British history. Despite this, the UK government under Tony Blair joined the US-led coalition that invaded Iraq in March 2003. The stated justification was that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction (WMD) that posed an imminent threat. No such weapons were found.

The Chilcot Inquiry, published in July 2016, was the most comprehensive public examination of the decision to go to war. Sir John Chilcot’s report concluded that the intelligence on Iraqi WMD was presented with more certainty than the evidence warranted; that the decision to invade was made before all peaceful options had been exhausted; that post-war planning was wholly inadequate; and that the legal basis for war was “far from satisfactory.” The report did not use the word “illegal” but concluded that the process for reaching the decision to go to war was flawed. The war divided British political opinion more sharply than any conflict since Suez (1956) and contributed to a lasting decline in public trust in political leaders.

The 7 July 2005 London bombings were carried out by four British-born men who detonated bombs on three Underground trains and a bus during the morning rush hour, killing 52 people and injuring over 700. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in Britain since Lockerbie (1988). The bombers had been inspired by al-Qaeda ideology and had links to conflicts in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The attacks prompted extensive debate about the relationship between British foreign policy (the Iraq War) and domestic terrorist recruitment.

The government’s response included the Counter-Terrorism Acts from 2000 onwards — extended by the Prevention of Terrorism Act (2005), the Terrorism Act (2006) and subsequent legislation. These raised questions about the balance between security and civil liberties: pre-charge detention was extended to 28 days (later reduced), control orders restricted individuals’ movements, and mass surveillance capabilities were expanded. Britain’s deployment in Afghanistan (2001–14) and Iraq (2003–09) represented the most sustained military commitments since the Falklands War (1982), and resulted in 179 and 456 British military deaths respectively.

Key Fact

The Chilcot Inquiry (published July 2016) concluded that the intelligence on Iraqi WMD was presented with more certainty than the evidence warranted, and that the decision to invade was taken before all peaceful options had been exhausted. Post-war planning was assessed as wholly inadequate.

before.exam_tip_html: For Change and Continuity essays, the post-1945 period offers a theme running through all three case studies: the tension between state security and individual rights. CND challenged nuclear deterrence policy; the Troubles raised questions about British Army conduct; the Iraq War and counter-terrorism legislation raised questions about civil liberties. Use the Chilcot Report as a specific named source for Iraq — examiners expect you to cite authoritative conclusions, not just describe events. For the Troubles, use the language of the Good Friday Agreement (‘consent’, ‘peaceful means’) and the Saville Inquiry’s findings — avoid asserting motives for events that remain politically contested.
